hypotheses.title: Coverage-First Round-Robin Passes
hypotheses.claim: Appending exactly this instruction — 'Use round-robin coverage passes: first remove every stub and implement the smallest specification-valid path in every module; only then revisit modules in descending risk to add boundary and error clauses, never polishing one module while another required behavior remains wholly unimplemented.' — will increase all-modules held-out pass rate under a fixed deadline relative to no appended instruction.
hypotheses.rationale: Coding agents often follow prompt order and sink time into locally difficult details, leaving later modules untouched; an all-or-nothing bundle then converts concentrated progress into failure. The instruction changes scheduling, not the implementation method: it lowers catastrophic omission risk by establishing a functional floor everywhere, then allocates remaining time by risk. It adds almost no explicit planning artifact or tool calls. weaknesses: No evidence is supplied that final-quarter reservation, clock awareness, or shortest-first repair improves this benchmark population.
The treatment combines three mechanisms--time reservation, cross-module rereading, and shortest-first prioritization--so a positive result would not identify which component caused it.
Final-quarter timing is not operationally precise for agents without a visible clock, and the instruction does not define what to do when the critical path is still incomplete at the cutoff.
Shortest clearly missing behavior is a convenience heuristic rather than an impact heuristic; it may consume the reserve on low-value clauses while a larger grading-critical omission remains.

hypothesis.title: Coverage-First Round-Robin Passes
hypothesis.claim: Appending exactly this instruction — 'Use round-robin coverage passes: first remove every stub and implement the smallest specification-valid path in every module; only then revisit modules in descending risk to add boundary and error clauses, never polishing one module while another required behavior remains wholly unimplemented.' — will increase all-modules held-out pass rate under a fixed deadline relative to no appended instruction.
hypothesis.rationale: Coding agents often follow prompt order and sink time into locally difficult details, leaving later modules untouched; an all-or-nothing bundle then converts concentrated progress into failure. The instruction changes scheduling, not the implementation method: it lowers catastrophic omission risk by establishing a functional floor everywhere, then allocates remaining time by risk. It adds almost no explicit planning artifact or tool calls.
assumptions: Baseline agents sometimes leave later modules or behavior classes untouched
A minimal valid path can be identified without causing large rework
Held-out grading rewards partial cross-module coverage enough to improve whole-bundle success
Risk ordering after the first pass is better than prompt-order polishing

Many residual failures are short omitted clauses discoverable by specification-to-code comparison
A final-quarter reserve is enough to repair at least one consequential omission
Stopping design work does not abandon a necessary deep implementation
